A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FORLA with the same core architecture and seven-dataset study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated between the main text and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original object-discovery experiments on surgical and natural datasets, including quantitative comparisons, distillation and personalization studies, and additional backbone, decoder, and video analyses in the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original partitioning, full-SAM comparison, foundation-model-count, and zero-shot transfer results in Figure 3 and Tables 5–7, 12, and 15.

M1.justification: The frozen foundation features, three adapter designs, student/teacher reconstruction objectives, and EMA followed by local/global FedAvg remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves into the main text with explanatory comments. The newly disclosed switching threshold and three-versus-four-model ablation do not establish a revised proposed method.

E1.justification: The same seven datasets and surgical/natural domains remain. Appendix G.6 adds a distinct zero-shot transfer scenario from PASCAL or YTOBJ to Abdominal images. New client partitions and data fractions change evaluation settings rather than dataset coverage; robotic manipulation remains future work.

E2.justification: Table 7 substantially extends comparison scope by evaluating complete SAM ViT-B and ViT-H segmenters with mask decoders; v1 used SAM features within slot-attention models instead. Table 15 also introduces source-trained zero-shot slot-attention comparators. The original comparator sets in the retained tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include two- and four-domain combinations, splitting each surgical domain between two clients, and four-client experiments using 25% or 10% of a domain per client. Additional settings compare three versus four foundation models, full SAM variants, and cross-domain zero-shot transfer. These extend evaluation design without establishing reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained distillation, personalization, and decoder studies, v2 tests sensitivity to domain combinations and client partitioning (Figure 3, Tables 5–6), the contribution of a fourth foundation model (Table 12), and natural-to-surgical transfer failure (Table 15). These substantially expand analysis of robustness and component necessity.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added results continue using point estimates, and Figure 3 has no uncertainty bars.

E6.justification: The matched original tables retain their numerical values, but v2 adds substantial results in Figure 3 and Tables 5–7, 12, and 15, plus timing measurements. For example, Table 6 reports PASCAL mBO of 32.09 for FORLA versus 34.99 for centralized training under the 10%-per-client setting. The new Table 7 reports FORLA PASCAL CorLoc as 45.04, conflicting with 64.84 in retained Table 1.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same feature construction, losses, aggregation rule, and slot-attention updates. Neither version adds theorems, proofs, formal assumptions, or substantive mathematical derivations; the algorithm relocation and comments are explanatory.

C1.justification: The principal federated object-centric learning and superiority claims remain. v2 explicitly frames novelty around demonstrating the approach at scale across expert and natural domains and specifies reference approaches for communication savings. The headline 7.6%, 85.2%, and 6.7× claims already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive applicability boundary: federated advantages weaken when local datasets are excessively partitioned or scarce. It also explains domain-dependent teacher benefits through foundation-model pretraining, discusses SAM's natural-versus-thoracic performance, and weighs additional backbone cost against representation quality. The original hierarchical-compositionality and foundation-model-dependence limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the 90,000-iteration stage switch, surgical slot-count tuning, and centralized training time. It names Toronto General Hospital and changes the thoracic-data footnote from a promised release to reported benchmark integration. The conflicting main-text weight decay of 1×10−5 disappears, while the appendix's existing 4×10−4 remains; this does not establish changed training.

R1.justification: v2 adds contextual citations and discussion of MONET, CTRL-O, SPOT, contrasting-slot learning, RADIOv2.5, recent surgical slot models, and prospective DINOv3/DROID use. The central positioning between federated learning and object-centric representation learning remains intact. The additional IODINE bibliography entry duplicates work already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The document substantially redistributes material: Algorithm 1 moves into the main method, adapter descriptions and detailed dataset descriptions move into appendices, and the main experimental setup is condensed. The supplement is reorganized from A.1–A.6 into sections A–H, alongside prose editing and expanded introductory explanation.

P2.justification: v2 adds the six-panel Figure 3 and five new tables, substantially expanding the visual presentation of evidence. Existing tables are regrouped, the author block is compacted, and diagram labels and captions are refined. Earlier video and PCA figures are retained, renumbered, and repositioned rather than replaced by new qualitative results.

improvement.justification: The new partitioning and data-scarcity tests examine an important assumption left largely untested in v1 and clarify when federated training helps. The backbone ablation and disclosed stage-switch threshold also improve justification and reproducibility. These benefits outweigh the added reporting problems, but the unexplained PASCAL CorLoc discrepancy in Table 7 and continued absence of uncertainty reporting limit confidence in the expanded evidence.
